papers.title_in_file: Quantum circuit complexity and unsupervised machine learning of topological order
papers.version_note: arXiv:2508.04486v2, dated 16 January 2026; the text layer holds the main text and the Supplementary Information once.
papers.what_it_is: A theory-and-simulation paper that proposes Nielsen's quantum circuit complexity as a distance for unsupervised manifold learning of topological order, proves two lower-bound theorems, and tests fidelity and entanglement kernels on tensor-network ground states.

existing.note: The robustness result is for two-qubit Haar random unitaries applied to the toric code and random product states (32 qubits, 20 samples, small proof-of-principle), not for noise in general. The supplement says noise in general invalidates the unitary-path ansatz.
existing.value: The authors report that, for the toric code ground state and random product states, the entanglement-based kernel is more robust than the fidelity-based kernel under the application of two-qubit Haar random unitaries.
existing.anchor: Section II.D.2, Fig. 3, p.8; Supplementary Sec. V, p.18
quotes: while the entanglement-based one is more robust under the application of two-qubit Haar random unitaries to both the toric code and the RPS
Generically, the presence of noise invalidates our original ansatz of unitary path planning
existing.certainty_reason: low: an empirical result from one small study
existing.reader_inference: The abstract says "local Haar random noises". The experiment applies layers of two-qubit Haar random gates to a 32-qubit system; this is a stand-in for noise, not a hardware noise model.

existing.note: The result holds for one fixed setting of the bond-alternating XXZ chain (large chain from DMRG, fixed field and detuning, 30 samples) and for both kernels together; the paper also notes an outlier in the critical region.
existing.value: The authors report that, for the bond-alternating XXZ chain solved by DMRG, the unsupervised learning produces distinct clusters associated with three phases (trivial, symmetry broken, and topological), in good agreement with independent calculations of topological invariants, using n = 151 qubits, h0 = 0 and delta = 3, with N = 30 samples drawn in J2/J1.
quotes: we find that the unsupervised learning produces distinct clusters that can be associated with three phases (trivial, symmetry broken, and topological), in good agreement with independent calculations of topological invariants
We use n = 151 qubits
We set h0 = 0 and δ = 3, while N = 30 samples are drawn uniformly
existing.certainty_reason: low: an empirical result from one study

assertions.value: The paper defines the quantum path planning problem as: given two arbitrary pure n-qubit quantum states, find continuous paths of the form of a unitary applied to the first state that connect the two states, where the generator of the unitary is a Hermitian operator with finite operator norm.
quotes: Definition 1. [Quantum path planning (QPP).] The QPP problem is defined as: Given two arbitrary pure n-qubit quantum states
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the paper states its own definition in Definition 1
assertions.reader_inference: The definition is the basis for every later bound.

assertions.value: The paper defines Nielsen's quantum circuit complexity of the first order for qubit systems as the infimum, over paths, of the integral of the sum of the absolute values of the real Pauli-expansion coefficients of the generator, and notes it can be generalized to other systems with an orthonormal operator basis of bounded operator norm.
quotes: Definition 3. (Nielsen's QCC.) The quantum circuit complexity of the unitary U (s = 1) can be evaluated through Nielsen's geometric approach
the Nielsen's quantum circuit complexity of the first order reads
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the paper states its own definition in Definition 3

assertions.value: The paper defines the quantum Fisher complexity as an infimum over paths of an integral of the square root of the quantum Fisher information, states that it represents the optimal Bures distance between the two states, and states that it coincides with the Bures distance given by a fidelity measure.
quotes: First, we define the quantum Fisher complexity (QFC) related to the QPP, denoted by CF (ρ0 → ρ1), which coincides with the Bures distance between the two quantum states given by a fidelity measure
which represents the optimal Bures distance between the two quantum states [81], reflecting the overall fidelity variation
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the paper states its own definition in Definition 4
assertions.reader_inference: The text calls the quantity "coincides with the Bures distance" in one place and "optimal Bures distance" in another; the supplement proves only the inequality chain.

assertions.value: The paper states Theorem 1: the Nielsen quantum circuit complexity for the quantum path planning between two states is lower bounded by the quantum Fisher complexity, which is lower bounded by the Bures distance; and for a geometrically local quantum circuit it is approximately lower bounded by a sum, over non-overlapping constant-size subsystems that together with their neighboring environments cover the whole system, of the Bures distance between the reduced density matrices.
assertions.anchor: Theorem 1, Section II.B, p.6; proof in Supplementary Sec. I, p.13-15
quotes: The QCC for the QPP from ρ0 to ρ1 is lower bounded by the QFC and the Bures distance
the QCC of a geometrically local quantum circuit for the same QPP is approximately lower bounded by
where ρ (∆) is the reduced density matrix supported on the subsystem ∆ of constant size
non-overlapping subsystems which, together with their neighboring environments, cover the whole system
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the statement and its conditions (geometric locality, constant-size subsystems, approximate bound) are quoted from Theorem 1, and the proof is in Supplementary Sec. I
assertions.reader_inference: The local bound uses an approximate sign and a Trotter-step argument, so it is not an exact inequality. The title of Theorem 1 says "upper bounds" while the body states lower bounds.

assertions.value: The authors state that the proof of the first theorem uses a Trotter decomposition of the unitary evolution into many small steps and the fact that the quantum Fisher information of a reduced density matrix does not exceed that of the enlarged pure system.
assertions.anchor: Supplementary Sec. I, proof of Theorem 1, p.14-15
quotes: We make a Trotter decomposition of the unitary evolution generated by G(s) into a product of many sufficiently small, finite time steps.
The QFI of the reduced density matrix with respect to s does not exceed that of its enlarged pure system
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the paper states the proof steps in the supplement

assertions.value: The paper states the second theorem: the Nielsen quantum circuit complexity for the quantum path planning from one n-qubit state to another with a geometrically local quantum circuit, with respect to the n-qubit chain, is lower bounded by a constant c times the average over the cuts of the absolute change in the entanglement entropy across each cut, for some constant c greater than zero.
assertions.anchor: Theorem 2, Section II.B, p.6-7; proof in Supplementary Sec. I, p.15
quotes: The QCC for the QPP from ρ0 to ρ1 with a geometrically local quantum circuit (with respect to the n-qubit chain) is lower bounded by
for some constant c > 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the statement and its condition (geometric locality along the chain, some constant c) are quoted from Theorem 2
assertions.reader_inference: The title of Theorem 2 says "upper bounds" while the body states a lower bound.

assertions.value: The authors state that the proof of Theorem 2 assumes the coupling in the generator between a subsystem and its environment is spatially local along the chain, relies on rigorous Small Incremental Entangling results from earlier work, and obtains the constant c as 1 over the product of a constant c-prime and the natural log of 2.
assertions.anchor: Supplementary Sec. I, proof of Theorem 2, p.15
quotes: we assume that the coupling in the generator G(s) of U (s) between Ak and Bk is spatially local with respect to the qubit chain
With rigorous results already proved in [112–116] concerning the Small Incremental Entangling (SIE)
for some constant c = 1/ (c′ ln 2) > 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the paper states the proof assumptions in the supplement

assertions.value: The authors define a fidelity-based kernel from the Uhlmann-Jozsa fidelity between r-body reduced density matrices up to a cutoff scale R, and an entanglement-based kernel from the entanglement-profile distance of Theorem 2, and state the entanglement kernel is particularly useful when the entanglement profile over nontrivial bonds can be efficiently estimated.
quotes: The Uhlmann-Jozsa fidelity between the r-body reduced density matrices with r = {1, 2, · · · , R} can be used for this purpose, where R is a scale of cutoff.
Theorem 2 inspires an entanglement-based kernel
which is particularly useful when the entanglement profile over nontrivial bonds can be efficiently estimated
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the paper states its own kernel definitions

assertions.value: The authors argue that Nielsen's quantum circuit complexity represents an intrinsic topological distance or similarity measure between topological phases, and propose an exponential kernel of the complexity, with a positive hyperparameter, as the theoretically optimal similarity for unsupervised manifold learning of topological order.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Section II.A, Eq. (3), p.5
quotes: We argue that Nielsen's quantum circuit complexity represents an intrinsic topological distance or similarity measure between topological quantum many-body phases of matter
up to a normalization constant, where β > 0 is a hyperparameter.
assertions.certainty_reason: low: the authors' argument; the exact complexity is not computed in the paper
assertions.reader_inference: The paper states that the exact complexity is generically intractable and tests only the two lower-bound substitutes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the shadow kernel suggested in earlier work can be understood as a special case of the fidelity-based kernel if the states and reduced density matrices are represented by their classical shadows, with the weight function set to nu to the r over r factorial and the limit R to infinity.
quotes: can be understood as a special case of the fidelity-based kernel in (10), if the quantum state ρ and the r-body reduced density matrices are represented by their classical shadows
assertions.certainty_reason: low: the authors' derivation is stated, not worked out in the text

assertions.value: The authors report that, for 10 toric code samples and 10 random product state samples on 32 qubits (a 4 by 4 lattice with toric boundary conditions), solved with DMRG, both kernels cluster the toric code and the random product states well with no noise.
quotes: We use N = 20 samples in total, with 10 samples of the toric code (blue dots) and 10 samples of the RPS
We use n = 32 qubits (on a lattice of size 4 × 4 with toric boundary condtions
The result shows that, in the absence of noise (i.e. with circuit depth zero), both kernels types perform well in clustering the toric code and the RPS
assertions.certainty_reason: low: an empirical result from one small proof-of-principle study
assertions.reader_inference: Twenty samples on one 32-qubit lattice is a small test; the authors call it a proof of principle.

assertions.value: The authors report that, for the extended toric code on an infinite cylinder of circumference 4 with 20 samples (10 of the extended toric code), the topological clustering with both kernels is robust to local perturbations, and that a maximal MPS bond dimension of 600 was sufficient for accurate results.
quotes: The result shows that the topological clustering is robust to local perturbations.
a maximal bond dimension of 600 is sufficient to produce accurate results
with a circumference of Ly = 4
We use N = 20 samples in total, with 10 samples of the ETC
assertions.certainty_reason: low: an empirical result from one small study

assertions.value: The authors state that for gapped ground states the quantum Fisher complexity is asymptotically tight as a lower bound of Nielsen's complexity, that the entanglement-based bound is asymptotically tight for the toric code ground state while the fidelity-based bound overestimates the circuit cost, and that for states whose complexity may grow exponentially with the number of qubits both bounds are no longer tight.
quotes: we will show in the following that the quantum Fisher complexity (QFC) in Theorem 1 is asymptotically (with respect to the number of qubits n) tight as a lower bound of the Nielsen's QCC
our entanglement-based bound is asymptotically tight for the toric code ground state, while the fidelity-based one overestimates the quantum circuit cost
both lower bounds [see Eq. (9) in Theorem 1 and Eq. (12) in Theorem 2] are no longer tight in this case
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the paper states where the bounds are tight and where they are not, in Supplementary Sec. III

assertions.value: The authors estimate Nielsen's complexity along a gapped Hamiltonian path in terms of the maximal operator norm of the path derivative of the Hamiltonian divided by the spectral gap, and state this is similar but not identical to the adiabaticity condition; the explicit optimization by differential geometry is left for further investigation.
quotes: where H(s) is the Hamiltonian path with a spectral gap δ(s) ≥ γ > 0 (∀s ∈ [0, 1])
which is similar (but not identical) to the adiabaticity condition in adiabatic quantum computation [117]
the Nielsen QCC may be explicitly obtained by optimization based on differential geometry, which deserves further investigation
assertions.certainty_reason: low: an order estimate stated without a full derivation of the constants

assertions.value: The authors state that the kernel computation with two-body reduced density matrices of constant size has computational or measurement complexity linear in the number of qubits, that kernel PCA and the diffusion map cost is cubic in the number of samples, and that metric-MDS or t-SNE is more suitable for large data sets with cost proportional to the iteration count times the square of the number of samples.
quotes: the computational or the measurement complexity in calculating the kernel is O(n)
the (classical) computational complexity of the kernel PCA and the diffusion map (manifold learning) algorithm is O N 3
the computational complexity of which is O(T N 2), where T is the number of iterations in the learning algorithm
assertions.certainty_reason: low: the authors' scaling statements; exponents are printed flat in the text layer

assertions.value: The authors state that estimating the quantum Fisher information and von Neumann entropy through classical shadows requires high-order moments of the density matrix which in general need exponentially many copies, that polynomially many local measurements may suffice for the second-order moment, that this remains open for the von Neumann entropy and the quantum Fisher information, and that they therefore conclude topological order is hard to learn in the worst case.
quotes: which in general require exponentially many copies of the quantum states
while it remains open for the Von Neumann entropy and the QFI, which deserves further investigations
Therefore, we may conclude that topological order is hard to learn in the worst case.
assertions.certainty_reason: low: the authors' conclusion from cited results

assertions.value: The authors state that decoherence during path planning invalidates the unitary-path ansatz and that a proper distance between noisy states may need the complexity of local quantum channels, which they leave for future work.
quotes: Generically, the presence of noise invalidates our original ansatz of unitary path planning, where the optimal distance is defined on a unitary-group manifold.

Proper topological distance between noisy quantum states may require the analysis of the complexity of local quantum channels, a generalization of our current approach, which we leave for future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the paper states this limit of its own approach in Supplementary Sec. V

assertions.value: The authors state that the demonstrated examples focus on pure and gapped ground states, and that gapless, topological quantum critical and mixed-state cases are possible extensions.
quotes: Also, in the demonstrated examples, so far we focused on pure and gapped ground states.
Possible extensions could be applications in gappless, topological quantum criticalities
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the paper states the scope of its examples

assertions.value: The authors state that, when limited to symmetry-protected topological order and compared with a recent neural-network result on the bond-alternating XXZ model, their method is fully unsupervised and gives sharper phase boundaries while providing good interpretability.
quotes: our method is fully unsupervised and results in sharper phase boundaries in clustering quantum phases of this model while providing good interpretability
assertions.certainty_reason: low: the authors' comparison to a cited work; no side-by-side numbers in this paper

assertions.value: The authors state that their approach is primarily classical machine learning of topological quantum order, and that quantum machine learning with parameterized circuits is an idea for future exploration.
quotes: Our current approach is primarily based on the classical machine learning of topological quantum order by exploiting Nielsen's QCC as an informational distance.
It might also be interesting to explore quantum machine learning [105, 106] in terms of parametrized quantum circuits
assertions.certainty_reason: high: the paper states the classical nature of its current approach
assertions.reader_inference: All numerical results use classical DMRG tensor-network simulation; no quantum hardware or quantum-circuit learning is run.

papers.title_in_file: Variational Quantum Circuits for Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.version_note: arXiv:1907.00397v3, 20 July 2020 (IEEE Access style); the text layer holds the paper twice, the second copy used only to check quotes.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation paper that trains variational-quantum-circuit Q-networks with experience replay and a target network on frozen-lake and cognitive-radio tasks, with a noisy simulation and a few inference runs on IBM hardware.

existing.note: The convergence figure is for the first of three channel-pattern configurations and a simple periodic primary-user pattern. The Fig. 8 caption says the 2-channel and 5-channel cases reach a reward of 100 and the 3-channel and 4-channel cases reach near-optimal, while the text says optimal at about 100 episodes.
existing.value: The authors report that in the cognitive-radio experiment, with 2, 3, 4 and 5 possible channels in the first configuration, they run 500 episodes and the agent converges to the optimal total reward value at around 100 iterations or episodes, while the figure caption states that the three-channel and four-channel cases reach a near-optimal policy.
existing.anchor: Section VI-D, p.14; Fig. 8 caption, p.12
quotes: there are 2, 3, 4 and 5 possible channels with the environment configuration shown in (a) of Fig. 3 for the agent to choose, respectively
we run 500 episodes and the agent converges to the optimal total reward value at around 100 iterations or episodes
the agent also reaches near-optimal policy at only several iterations
existing.certainty_reason: low: an empirical result from one study run in classical simulation

existing.note: The noise result is a classical Qiskit Aer simulation with a noise model downloaded from one IBM machine on one date, for the 2-channel and 4-channel settings only. The paper separately ran inference with the trained noiseless model on real hardware.
existing.value: The authors report that in a simulation using noise data downloaded from the IBM Q machine ibmq-poughkeepsie, for the 2-channel and 4-channel cognitive-radio settings, the agent converges to the optimal total reward value at around 110 iterations, and they conclude their quantum circuit based DRL is robust against noise in the current machines.

existing.value: The authors state that for the considered testing environments variational quantum deep Q-learning involves parameters as small as O(n), against tabular Q-learning and neural network based deep Q-learning with O(n3) and O(n2) parameters (printed flat; n cubed and n squared), and that the scaling comparison is restricted to the cases they test, with the number of channels n up to 5.

papers.title_in_file: Efficient Postprocessing Procedure for Evaluating Hamiltonian Expectation Values in Variational Quantum Eigensolver
papers.version_note: arXiv:2312.01023v2, 27 December 2023. The PDF has 7 pages; the text layer holds the 3-page-plus-appendix paper twice (two-column reading order is interleaved in places), the second copy used only to check quotes. The record title says 'More Efficient'; the file title is 'Efficient Postprocessing Procedure'.
papers.what_it_is: A short VQE software-method paper proposing a measurement-memory dictionary that caches the eigenvalue of each commuting group for each measured bit string, with a complexity argument and CPU-time simulations.

existing.note: The speedup is the order of growth of the percentage of CPU time saved, observed for up to 20 qubits, with a fitted quadratic label on the figure; the percentage cannot exceed 100 so it is not an asymptotic claim; and it is a classical simulation timing.
existing.value: The authors report that, for a fully connected Ising Hamiltonian up to 20 qubits, where all O(N2) terms commute (exponents printed flat), the method offers an O(N2) speedup in terms of the percentage of time saved; the run uses 10 initial parameter guesses, 200 optimization steps, and Fig. 1 carries the label 0.16x2 - 1.65x + 4.15.
existing.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Section IV.A, Fig. 1, p.2-3
quotes: For Ising Hamiltonian, where all O(N 2) terms commute, our method offers an O(N 2) speedup in terms of the percentage of time saved.
minimizing a fully connected Ising Hamiltonians up to 20 qubits
We take 10 initial parameter guesses
CPU time (t ) for 200 steps of optimization of fully-connected Ising Hamiltonians
existing.certainty_reason: low: an empirical result from one study
existing.reader_inference: The O(N2) is a growth order of a percentage over 20 qubits (a fitted quadratic label on Fig. 1b), not a proved asymptotic speedup.

existing.note: The appendix proves MM is no worse than the sort-and-evaluate procedure (worst case equal when nothing is stored, and each stored state trades a cost of order N plus the group cost for twice the order of N), which relies on the group evaluation cost being at least order N. It does not show MM beats naive evaluation in every case, and it analyses time only.
existing.value: The authors state that, in the appendix, in the worst case the first step with no stored bit strings has the complexity equal to the sort-and-evaluate scheme, and that for every extra state stored they trade a cost of order N plus the group evaluation cost for two times a cost of order N, which they take as showing MM is more efficient than the sort-and-evaluate procedure.
existing.anchor: Abstract, p.1; Appendix, Time Complexity of MM, p.4-5
quotes: In equation 14, we can see that in the worst case, for example, the first step, l = 0, the complexity is equal to sort-and-evaluate scheme
For every extra state we store (i.e. l + 1), we are trading O (N ) + O (G) cost for 2O (N ).
Since O (G) ≥ O (N ) in general
